name: Towers Financial Corporation

summary.text: Towers Financial Corporation was a New York-based factoring and debt-collection company run by Steven Hoffenberg. On February 8, 1993 the SEC sued Towers, Hoffenberg and two other executives in the Southern District of New York (93 Civ. 0744), alleging an unregistered offering of promissory notes and material misrepresentations about the company's finances; the company filed for Chapter 11 in March 1993. The SEC later described the case as one of the largest Ponzi schemes in history, with investor losses of close to half a billion dollars. Hoffenberg pleaded guilty in April 1995 and was sentenced in March 1997 to 20 years in prison and about $475 million in restitution. Jeffrey Epstein worked as a consultant to the firm from about 1987 and was never charged; Hoffenberg's later claims that Epstein designed the fraud were made in interviews and in suits that were withdrawn.

facts.claim: On February 8, 1993 the SEC filed a civil injunctive action in the Southern District of New York (SEC v. Towers Financial Corporation, Steven Hoffenberg, Mitchell Brater and Arthur Ferro, 93 Civ. 0744) alleging that Towers, a factoring concern, Hoffenberg and Brater were engaged in an illegal unregistered offering of promissory notes and had made material misrepresentations about Towers' financial condition, including overstating collection receivables and fee income.
facts.quote: The Commission's complaint alleges that Towers, a factoring concern, Hoffenberg and Brater have been engaged in an illegal unregistered offering of promissory notes.

sources.title: SEC News Digest, Issue 93-25
Litigation Release No. 15053

facts.claim: The SEC's complaint alleged Hoffenberg made false and misleading statements to investors who had purchased $215 million in Towers promissory notes and sold Towers stock while holding inside information that it was worthless; on March 3, 1993 the SEC amended the complaint to allege that Towers, through subsidiaries, fraudulently sold almost $200 million of securities. Towers filed for Chapter 11 protection in March 1993.
facts.quote: The amended complaint alleges that Towers, through its subsidiaries, fraudulently sold almost $200 million of securities.

facts.claim: In February 1994 the SEC described the criminal charges against Hoffenberg as defrauding Towers investors of close to half a billion dollars and accused Hoffenberg and Towers of operating one of the largest Ponzi schemes in history.
facts.quote: The SEC charged Hoffenberg with defrauding investors in Towers of close to half a billion dollars, and accused Hoffenberg and Towers of operating one of the largest Ponzi schemes in history.

facts.claim: Hoffenberg pleaded guilty on April 20, 1995 to conspiring to commit securities fraud; in his plea allocution he admitted knowing that Towers' financial statements overstated its assets and revenues and that prospectuses mailed to investors carried those statements. The 1998 noteholders' litigation relied on the plea for summary judgment against him.
facts.quote: Hoffenberg pled guilty to this count, and the opinion cites a plea allocution transcript dated April 20, 1995.

facts.claim: On March 7, 1997 Judge Robert W. Sweet sentenced Hoffenberg to twenty years' imprisonment, three years of supervised release, a $1 million fine and approximately $475 million in restitution ($475,157,340 per a later New Jersey district court ruling).
facts.quote: On March 7, 1997, this Court sentenced Hoffenberg to twenty years' imprisonment, followed by a three-year term of supervised release, as well as a $1 million fine, approximately $475 million in restitution, and a $50 special assessment on each of the five counts.

facts.claim: Towers victims recovered very little: the Daily Beast, quoting the New York Times, reported that the money is gone and those defrauded got back less than a penny for every dollar they lost.
facts.quote: the money is gone, and those he defrauded got back less than a penny for every dollar they lost.

facts.claim: Hoffenberg hired Jeffrey Epstein as a consultant to Towers from about 1987 to 1993 at $25,000 a month, with a $2 million loan in 1988 that Epstein did not have to repay, according to CBS News; a lawyer for the investors' committee described Epstein as effectively the firm's number two or three person.
facts.quote: "As I understood, he was sort of a senior VP. If he was not the number two guy, he was certainly the number two or number three person at the firm," said Terrence Corrigan, a lawyer for a committee tasked with getting back money for an estimated 2,800 investors in the scam.

facts.claim: Hoffenberg alleged that in 1987 and 1988 Epstein ran a scheme to finance Towers' unsuccessful takeover bids for Pan American World Airways and Emery Air Freight using cash from two Illinois insurance companies that Towers had promised regulators it would keep solvent. This is Hoffenberg's allegation; it was not adjudicated.

openQuestions: The headline loss figure varies: $215 million in notes (1993 complaint), 'almost $200 million' (amended complaint), 'close to half a billion' (SEC 1994), $460-463 million (press/Wikipedia) and $475,157,340 (restitution order). The site's '$450M' is within this range but no source gives that exact figure.

The full text of SEC Litigation Release 13514 and the 1997 sentencing opinion (1997 WL 96563) were not retrieved; the SEC News Digests and later court opinions are cited instead. Whether a TRO was granted in February 1993 is not confirmed.
Epstein's start date: most sources say 1987; one account citing the New York Times says 1983. Departure: 'by 1989' vs. 'about 1993' in different reports.

Hoffenberg's charges at plea are described variously (five counts; conspiracy to commit securities fraud; mail fraud, tax evasion and obstruction). The Justia 1998 opinion confirms the securities-fraud conspiracy count; the five-count structure is confirmed by the $50-per-count assessment in the sentencing description.

All claims about Epstein designing or profiting from the fraud rest on Hoffenberg (a convicted participant with an interest in shifting blame) and on withdrawn complaints; no court finding supports them.
